passages.text: A Shift in Myeloid Cell Phenotype via Down Regulation of Siglec-1 in Island Macrophages of Bone Marrow Is Associated With Decreased Late Erythroblasts Seen in Anemia of Critical Illness

Burn injury has been shown to significantly dampen erythropoiesis in both burn patients and in murine models. <sentence_start/>Our previous findings elucidated the erythropoietin independent defects in red cell development stages involving erythroid progenitor production and late stage erythroblast enucleation processes. <sentence_start/>We hypothesized that macrophages (MØ) in erythroblast islands (EBI) could be yet another roadblock impeding erythropoiesis following burn injury. <sentence_start/>Here we highlight that the methodology to study EBI can be achieved with single cell suspensions using a simple technique such as flow cytometry, as obtaining the central erythroblast island macrophages (EBIMØs) of interest is a delicate process. <sentence_start/>We elucidated the requisite of EBIMØ from the erythroblast as well as the MØ perspective. <sentence_start/>In addition to the primary erythropoiesis organ, the bone marrow (BM), spleens were also examined for extra-medullary erythropoiesis. <sentence_start/>Femurs and spleens were harvested from adult mice (B<sub>6</sub>D<sub>2</sub>F<sub>1</sub>) subjected to 15% total body surface area (TBSA) scald burn (B) or sham burn (S). <sentence_start/>Total bone marrow cells (TBM) and splenocytes were probed for total erythrons, early and late erythroblasts and EBIMØ by flow cytometry. <sentence_start/>There was only a marginal increase in the number of EBIMØ after burn, but, between the signatures of EBIMØ, Siglec-1 expression (MFI) was reduced by 40% in B with and a parallel 44% decrease in TBM erythrons in the BM. <sentence_start/>There were more (2.5-fold) EEBs and less LEBs (2.4-fold) per million TBM cells in B; with a corresponding decrease in Siglec-1 and Ly6G expressions in EBIMØ associated with EEB. <sentence_start/>Conversely, extra-medullary erythropoiesis was robust in spleens from B. <sentence_start/>Not only were the numbers of EBIMØs increased in B (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.002), both EEBs and LEBs associated with EBIMØ were higher by 30 and 75%, respectively. <sentence_start/>Importantly, an increase in Siglec-1 and Vcam1 expressing F480<sup>+</sup> splenic macrophages was observed after burn injury. <sentence_start/>Therefore, stagnant EEBs in the BM after burn injury could be due to low Siglec1 expressing EBIMØ, which perhaps impede their maturation into LEBs and reticulocytes. <sentence_start/>Repercussion of myeloid cell phenotype specific to BM after burn injury could plausibly account for a defective late stage RBC maturation resulting in anemia of critical illness.
<bold>Summary Sentence:</bold> Characterization of erythroblast island macrophages (EBIMØ) in the bone marrow and spleen at different stages of erythropoiesis after burn injury.
Introduction

Anemia, immune-suppression, and monocytosis are immune consequences of a traumatic burn injury (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00000658-199303000-00012" pmid="8452408" pmcid="PMC1242783" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00000658-200101000-00015" pmid="11141231" pmcid="PMC1421160" count="1">2</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, burn injury bifurcates the common myeloid progenitors toward granulocyte monocyte commitment by increasing MafB (myeloid transcription factor) expression and thereby reducing the production of megakaryocyte erythrocyte progenitors (MEP) (<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/TA.0b013e31822e2803" pmid="22071930" pmcid="PMC3217199" count="1">3</citation>-<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1189/jlb.0711338" pmid="21984745" pmcid="PMC3250307" count="1">5</citation>). <sentence_start/>Monocytes that mature into tissue macrophages (MØ) also serve a unique function of nurturing the erythroblasts during erythropoiesis (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3057" pmid="23502962" pmcid="PMC3983996" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1182/blood-2008-03-077883" pmid="18650462" pmcid="PMC2481536" count="1">7</citation>). <sentence_start/>Besides the hematopoietic shortcoming of bone marrow MEP commitment, it is not known whether myeloid cells stemming from burn-induced microenvironment also impede red blood cell development. <sentence_start/>As burn injury affects both the erythroid and myeloid arms of hematopoiesis resulting in Epo resistant anemia (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00000658-199303000-00012" pmid="8452408" pmcid="PMC1242783" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00004630-199109000-00008" pmid="1752878" count="1">8</citation>, <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/BCR.0000000000000592" pmid="28570310" pmcid="PMC5709235" count="1">9</citation>), we utilized this burn model to study the bearing of MØ phenotype in burn-mediated anemia of critical illness. <sentence_start/>The concept of erythroblast island macrophages (EBIMØ) has been known for more than 60 years (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" pmid="13555228" count="1">10</citation>) but not completely understood (<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1182/blood.V92.8.2940" pmid="9763581" count="1">11</citation>, <citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1182/blood-2007-06-098178" pmid="17993612" pmcid="PMC2214751" count="1">12</citation>). <sentence_start/>Recent <italic toggle="yes">in vitro</italic> evidence using time lapse video microscopy shows the interaction of macrophages with erythroblasts at various stages of maturation (<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3324/haematol.2013.094466" pmid="24186310" pmcid="PMC3815163" count="1">13</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, characterizing the phenotype of EBIMØ in burn pathology is essential to understand the efficacy of erythroblast islands contributing to the maturation of erythroblasts and to eventually underscore the intercellular signals.

For the characterization of EBIMØ, emerging studies point to multiple markers such as CD163, Ly6G, ERHR3, Vcam1, and Siglec1 associated with F4/80<sup>+</sup> macrophages (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3057" pmid="23502962" pmcid="PMC3983996" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exphem.2014.03.009" pmid="24721610" count="1">14</citation>-<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2017.01140" pmid="28979259" pmcid="PMC5611421" count="1">17</citation>). <sentence_start/>Due to the structural arrangement of an EBI in which the central macrophage is surrounded by immature erythroblasts, techniques like immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence do not provide both qualitative and quantitative information required for studying the changes occurring in these macrophages under different pathological conditions, while use of flow cytometry has provided significant information in the characterization of EBIMØs (<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2017.01140" pmid="28979259" pmcid="PMC5611421" count="1">17</citation>, <citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MOH.0000000000000131" pmid="25693142" count="1">18</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, in this study we predominantly screened EBIMØs using eight-color flow cytometry to comprehend the interference of macrophage abnormality during erythroblast maturation after burn injury. <sentence_start/>Moreover, under hypoxic conditions of burn injury, the spleen serves as an extra medullary erythropoietic organ in adult mice. <sentence_start/>Therefore, to compare and contrast erythropoiesis between the two organs in response to burn injury we also examined the phenotype of EBIMØ, the distribution of erythroblasts and RBCs in spleen. <sentence_start/>Of the two organs, EBIMØs in the spleen facilitate erythroblast maturation contributing to extra medullary erythropoiesis where as, bone marrow EBIMØ phenotype is certainly compromised resulting in the inhibition of erythroblast maturation.
Methods
Mouse Model of Burn Injury
Mice

Six to eight weeks old B6D2F1 male mice weighing ~25 g were purchased from Jackson Laboratories (Barr Harbor, ME). <sentence_start/>Mice were housed in our Comparative Medicine Facility with 12 h light/dark cycle with controlled temperature (20-22°C). <sentence_start/>The mice were allowed to acclimate to our facility for 7 days prior to use. <sentence_start/>The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Loyola University Medical Center approved all experimental protocols.
Burn Injury

B6D2F1 male mice were randomly divided into sham and burn groups. <sentence_start/>Mice were anesthetized using ketamine and xylazine (100, 2.5 mg/kg, respectively; intraperitoneal) and their dorsal hair was removed by shaving. <sentence_start/>Mice were subjected to a 15% TBSA full thickness scald burn along the dorsum by immersion in a 100°C water bath for 8 s (<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00005373-196811000-00006" pmid="5722120" count="1">19</citation>) and were resuscitated immediately with intra-peritoneal injection of normal saline (2 mL). <sentence_start/>A sham group of mice were administered anesthesia, shaved and resuscitated but were not subjected to burn injury. <sentence_start/>Animals were sacrificed either on post burn days 3, 7, 14, or 21 as indicated in the results section. <sentence_start/>All experiments were repeated four to five times.
Isolation of Total Bone Marrow Cells and Splenocytes

Total bone marrow cells from the bilateral femurs of each mouse were eluted into McCoy's medium (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) using a 25-gauge needle. <sentence_start/>Spleens were mashed with the back of a 3 ml syringe plunger and filtered through a 70 μm cell strainers to collect the splenocytes.
Antibodies Used

F4/80-biotin, clone BM8, cat # 48015 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), Anti-Biotin Microbeads, cat # 130-090-485; MS columns cat # 130-042-201 (Miltenyi Biotech, San Diego, CA), CD71-PE, C2 clone, cat # 553267 (BD Pharmigen, San Diego, CA), Ter119-PerCP Cy5.5 (clone Ter-119; cat # 45-5921-82; eBioscience, San Diego, CA), F4/80-PeCy7 (clone BM8; cat # 25-4801-82; eBioscience, San Diego, CA), ERHR3-Alexa fluor 700A; cat # MCA2393A488; Novusbio, Centennial, CO), CD169-APC (clone REA197; cat # 130-104-954; Miltenyi Biotec, San Diego, CA), CD106/VCAM1 - PacBlue, (clone 429 MVCAM.A; cat # 105722; Biolegend, San Diego, CA), Ly6G-APC Cy7 (clone 1A8; cat # 127624; Biolegend, San Diego, CA), Syto16-FITC (cat # S7578; Fischer Scientific, Waltham, MA), CD16/CD43 Mouse BD FC Block (clone 2.4G2 RUO; cat # 553141; BD Pharmingen, San Diego, CA), OneComp eBeads Compensation Beads (cat # 01-1111-41; Invitrogen/Fischer Scientific, Waltham, MA).
Magnetic Isolation of F4/80<sup>+</sup> Macrophages

Total bone marrow and spleen cells were stained with biotinylated F4/80 antibody. <sentence_start/>After 15 min of incubation at 4°C, the cells were washed and stained with anti-biotin microbeads. <sentence_start/>After 15 min of incubation at 4°C, the cells were washed and passed through the MS magnetic column (Milteneyi). <sentence_start/>F4/80<sup>+</sup> cells were collected from the column using a plunger.
Flow Cytometry

Total bone marrow cells and spleen cells were subjected to eight-color analysis (cocktail of eight antigens simultaneously); using a fluorescence activated cell-sorting (FACS) machine (LSR Fortessa 1 analyzer) and results from 150,000 events were archived. <sentence_start/>Data were obtained using Flow Jo software (Tree Star, Ashland, OR) from the viable cells gated based on forward scatter (FSC-A) and side scatter (SSC-A) and analyzed for the expression of various marker proteins using relevant antibodies as enumerated above. <sentence_start/>Positive and negative gates were set with FMO (fluorescent minus one) controls and unstained cells, respectively. <sentence_start/>Flurochrome compensation was performed using OneComp eBeads.
Confocal Microscopy

An aliquot of TBM cells were eluted using a 21-gauge needle from untreated sham mice was stained with Siglec1-PE and Ter119-FITC. <sentence_start/>The cells were then cytospun onto microscopic slides and preserved using Vectashield H-1500 mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA). <sentence_start/>A Zeiss LSM 510 laser-scanning microscope (Carl Zeiss MicroImaging, Jena, Germany) was used to view with C-Apochromat 403 1.20 water immersion, and X40 images were acquired using Zeiss LSM 510, version 4.2, SPI software.
Spleen Tissue Sections

Spleens from the sham and post burn day 7 mice were isolated and fixed in 10% formalin for at least 24 h, decalcified (only femurs) and stained using hematoxylin and eosin, according to standard techniques, by the Histology Core Facility of Loyola University Medical Center. <sentence_start/>Light microscopy was performed, and digital images were captured (× 10 and × 40 magnification).
Identification of Erythroblast Island Macrophages (EBIMØs) and Erythroblasts

A combination of markers were used to identify and quantify EBIMØ (F4/80<sup>pos</sup> ER-HR3<sup>pos</sup> Vcam1<sup>pos</sup> Siglec1<sup>pos</sup> and Ly6G<sup>pos/neg</sup>), total erythrons (CD71<sup>pos</sup> Ter119<sup>neg/pos</sup>), early erythroblasts (CD71<sup>pos</sup>Ter119<sup>neg</sup>), late erythroblasts (CD71<sup>pos</sup> Ter119<sup>pos</sup>), Orthochromatic/polychromatic erythroblasts (CD71<sup>pos</sup> Ter119<sup>pos</sup> Syto16<sup>pos</sup>), reticulocytes (CD71<sup>pos</sup> Ter119<sup>pos</sup> Syto16<sup>neg</sup>), and RBCs (CD71<sup>neg</sup> Ter119<sup>pos</sup>) (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.surg.2017.06.001" pmid="28716301" pmcid="PMC5675564" count="1">20</citation>).
Gating Strategy for Erythroblast Island Macrophage (EBIMØ)

To include all the macrophages that are present either in isolation or in association with erythroblasts, TBM cells and splenocytes were first gated on FCS-A and FSC-H (singlets and doublets) followed by F4/80 on x-axis and SSC-A on y-axis. <sentence_start/>Next, using histograms, we sequentially determined all the expected markers in the order of prevalence, ERHR3<sup>pos</sup> >Vcam1<sup>pos</sup> >Siglec1<sup>pos</sup> > Ly6G<sup>pos</sup>. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, F4/80<sup>pos</sup> cells were then gated to include ERHR3<sup>pos</sup> on x-axis and F4/80<sup>pos</sup> on y-axis. <sentence_start/>F4/80<sup>pos</sup> ERHR3<sup>pos</sup> cells were then gated on Vcam1<sup>pos</sup> on y-axis and Siglec1<sup>pos</sup> on x-axis. <sentence_start/>The dual positive cells predominantly constitute all EBIMØ (F4/80<sup>pos</sup> ERHR3<sup>pos</sup> Vcam1<sup>pos</sup> Siglec1<sup>pos</sup> and Ly6G<sup>pos/neg</sup>). <sentence_start/>We have made similar gating on F4/80<sup>neg</sup> cells to confirm this gating includes most of the EBIMØs. <sentence_start/>We found there are 5,000 times more EBIMØ in F4/80<sup>pos</sup> subset (see Supplemental Figure 1).
Gating Strategy for Erythrocytes and Erythroblast Subsets

Singlets/doublets were gated on CD71 and Ter119 to identify total erythrons (CD71<sup>pos</sup> Ter119<sup>neg/pos</sup>), which were then represented as x10<sup>3</sup> cells per million TBM cells. <sentence_start/>We then re-gated the total erythrons into RBCs (CD71<sup>neg</sup> Ter119<sup>pos</sup>), EEB (CD71<sup>pos</sup> Ter119<sup>neg</sup>) and LEB (CD71<sup>pos</sup> Ter119<sup>pos</sup>). <sentence_start/>There are two subsets within the LEBs; nucleated cells belong to polychromatic erythroblasts (PolyE) and orthochromatic erythroblasts (OrthoE) whereas those that lack a nucleus are reticulocytes that mature into RBCs in circulation. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we utilized the cell permeable nuclear dye Syto16 to delineate the two subsets (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.surg.2017.06.001" pmid="28716301" pmcid="PMC5675564" count="1">20</citation>). <sentence_start/>Supplemental Figure 2 compares identification of discrete erythroblasts using the above-mentioned method including Syto16 compared to the Koulnis et al. using FSC vs. CD71 (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3791/2809" pmcid="PMC3211121" pmid="21847081" count="1">21</citation>).
Blood Collection, Plasma Separation, and Hematrue for Blood Parameters

Peripheral blood. <sentence_start/>Heparinized blood samples from study groups were collected through cardiac puncture and examined on a veterinary hematology analyzer (HemaTrue, Heska, Love- land, CO), and RBC counts and hemoglobin levels were recorded. <sentence_start/>Plasma was separated from the blood after centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 10 min at 4°C.
Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA)

G-CSF levels were analyzed as a 10x fold dilution of study plasma in Diluent A from this commercially available kit according to the manufactures' instructions (cat# EMCSF3, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). <sentence_start/>All measurements were preformed in duplicates.
Statistical Analysis

Results from all experiments are expressed as mean ± sem. <sentence_start/>Number of animals used per experiment were 6-8 as given in respective figure legends. <sentence_start/>Plasma G-CSF results were determined using 4 mice per group. <sentence_start/>Analysis of variance with Tukey's <italic toggle="yes">post-hoc</italic> test using KaleidaGraph statistical program, version 4.1.0 (Synergy Software, Reading, PA, USA) were carried out for comparison between groups. <sentence_start/>Statistical significance was set at <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 0.05. <sentence_start/>All experiments were repeated 2-3 times.
Results
Medullary and Extramedullary Erythropoiesis During the Course of Burn Injury

We monitored the medullar and extra medullar erythropoietic responses from days 3 through 21 post burn. <sentence_start/>While extra medullar erythropoiesis was active through the course of burn injury starting from day 3, medullar erythropoiesis was significantly attenuated from day 7 as measured by the percentage of CD71<sup>+</sup>Ter119<sup>±</sup> cells in spleen and TBM. <sentence_start/>The ratio of reticulocytes to nucleated BM erythroblasts (maturation index) was significantly decreased from day 7 through day 21 as an indication of late maturation defects following burn injury. <sentence_start/>Further, during the same study period, F4/80<sup>+</sup> MØ in the BM showed deficiency in MØ associated adhesion molecule expression (Figures 1A-D). <sentence_start/>Therefore, we chose day 7 post burn to study the phenotype of EBIMØs and the stage specific association of erythroblasts in a comprehensive manner during medullar arrest and extra medullar excess in BM and spleen, respectively, to observe the status of EBI integrity.

Bone Marrow
Bone Marrow Erythroblast Island Macrophage Phenotype From a Macrophage Perspective

The percentage of EBIMØ was determined for each sample as explained in the methods section and back-calculated to represent absolute numbers in a million TBM cells. <sentence_start/>The total number of EBIMØ per million TBM cells was marginally higher in burn group compared to sham (S = 225 ± 4.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>, B = 264 ± 5.4 × 10<sup>3</sup>; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.002; Figure 2A). <sentence_start/>As this EBIMØ gating includes both Ly6G<sup>pos</sup> and Ly6G<sup>neg</sup> cells, we further gated these MØ on Ly6G and Siglec1 expressions. <sentence_start/>While there was an equal distribution of Ly6G<sup>pos</sup> and Ly6G<sup>neg</sup> MØs in this fraction (Figure 2B), we noticed a significant reduction in Siglec1 expression in EBIMØ from burn compared to sham (S = 2,977 ± 58, B = 1,913 ± 71; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.0001; Table 1). <sentence_start/>Moreover, we noticed a 40% reduction in Siglec1 expression irrespective of Ly6G<sup>pos</sup> or Ly6G<sup>neg</sup> EBIMØ from burn mice (Histograms in Figure 2C). <sentence_start/>We then documented the distribution of erythroblasts associated with these EBIMØ. <sentence_start/>As shown by contour plots in Figure 2D, there was a striking contrast in the type of erythroblasts nurtured by bone marrow EBIMØs from sham vs. burn mice. <sentence_start/>More EEBs from burn mice and more LEBs from sham mice were associated with EBIMØ. <sentence_start/>The mean fluorescent intensities of Ly6G, ERHR3, and VCAM1 expressions were similar between sham and burn EBIMØ isolated from the femurs (Table 1). <sentence_start/>These results still do not answer the importance of Siglec1 or Ly6G on EBIMØ.

Is Ly6G Expression Critical for Bone Marrow EBIMØ Association With Early and Late Erythroblasts?

To inquire the importance of Ly6G and its association with EEB and LEB in F4/80<sup>pos</sup> MØ, we utilized a machine-learning algorithm called T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) plots as shown in Figure 2E. Overall, comparing Ly6G<sup>lo</sup> vs. Ly6G<sup>hi</sup> MØ, Ly6G<sup>lo</sup> expressing MØ were predominantly associated with EEBs and LEBs irrespective of sham or burn conditions. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, among the F4/80<sup>pos</sup>Ly6G<sup>lo</sup> MØs, we noticed 3 times more LEB association in sham and 2.5 times more EEB association in burn groups.
Bone Marrow Total Erythrons and Erythroblast Subsets Are Altered After Burn

For overall comparison between two groups and to visualize flow data, we utilized t-sne plots denoting CD71<sup>+</sup> TBM cells. <sentence_start/>Bone marrow CD71<sup>lo−hi</sup> cells are a representation of erythroid staining obtained from six animals per group shown in t-sne plots (Figures 3A,B). <sentence_start/>We noticed a 2.8-fold decrease in the percentage of CD71<sup>hi</sup> bone marrow cells from burn group.

Discussion

Here, we have elucidated that burn injury perturbs bone marrow EBIMØ phenotype. <sentence_start/>Further, Siglec1 down-regulation emerges as a predominant deficit in EBIMØ after burn from both the erythroblast as well as the MØ perspective. <sentence_start/>In contrast to bone marrow EBIMØ, Ly6G, and ERHR3 are stronger in splenic EBIMØ while Siglec1 expression is not reduced in response to burn injury, sparing extra medullary erythropoiesis presenting the possibility of the interference of myeloid abnormality disrupting early to late erythroblast maturation.

The higher percentage of EEBs (2.5-fold) associated with low Siglec1 expressing EBIMØ after burn injury could probably mean an impaired differentiation to LEBs because, LEBs are also found to be reduced in the bone marrow of mice subjected to burns with a parallel increase in EEBs (2.4-fold) resulting in overall 45% reduction in total erythrons in line with our earlier report (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.surg.2017.06.001" pmid="28716301" pmcid="PMC5675564" count="1">20</citation>). <sentence_start/>Lack of MØ availability can be ruled out because there were no differences between sham and burn in the ratio of EEB and LEB to EBIMØ at 2:1 and 5:1, respectively. <sentence_start/>This could imply a specific role for Siglec1 during the process of differentiation from proerythroblasts to PolyE, OrthoE, and reticulocyte stages. <sentence_start/>One eminent function is to provide iron to the attached EEBs as EBIMØ have been shown to make iron available during erythroblast maturation (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2014.00009" pmid="24523696" pmcid="PMC3906564" count="1">22</citation>), but do not specify the role of Siglec1 in this process. <sentence_start/>Alternatively, one can speculate, Siglec1 is important for chromatin condensation or for the formation of contractile actin rings involved in nuclear pyknosis, all of which are needed during erythroblast maturation (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2017.01076" pmid="29311991" pmcid="PMC5742207" count="1">23</citation>). <sentence_start/>This speculation is further strengthened by our results from spleen where Siglec1 expression is maintained, and extramedullary response is robust, with more LEBs (2.4-fold) that are associated with EBIMØ, resulting in a 70% increase in overall splenic erythrons, with significant increases in EEBs (30%) and LEBs (75%) after burn.

Splenic responses to thermal injury have previously been reported when granulocytes, granulocyte-macrophages, and macrophage progenitors increase soon after thermal injury (14% TBSA), with maximal responses seen after a week (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/01.shk.0000154239.00887.18" pmid="15665725" count="1">24</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the same study they showed an increase in the number of marginal zone (CD115<sup>+</sup>) and not red pulp (F4/80<sup>+</sup>) macrophages after thermal burn, which matches with our current observation of insignificant increase in percentage of splenic F4/80<sup>+</sup> MØ on day 7 after burn (15% TBSA). <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, alterations in MØ phenotypes are quite possible in other models of burn injury as shown by an increase in CD11b<sup>+</sup>F4/80<sup>+</sup> peritoneal macrophages (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00000658-200211000-00016" pmid="12409672" pmcid="PMC1422624" count="1">25</citation>).

Splenic erythropoiesis is increased at the expense of medullar erythropoiesis when erythroid island macrophages were depleted simultaneously with G-CSF mobilization (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exphem.2014.03.009" pmid="24721610" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>Our results are supported by the above study because, we observed similar BM erythroid arrest in our model and additionally, burn patients have increased plasma levels of catecholamines and G-CSF (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/SHK.0b013e3181b92340" pmid="20407405" pmcid="PMC2858869" count="1">26</citation>) echoing a plausible G-CSF mediated response. <sentence_start/>Moreover, in the same study, CD169 specific depletion of MØ in G-CSF treated mice resulted in significant loss of reticulocytes with corresponding increase in the number of pro erythroblasts (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exphem.2014.03.009" pmid="24721610" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, our model of burn injury resulted in high numbers of stagnant EEBs after burn, with significant reduction in LEBs and reticulocytes, further strengthening our notion that late maturation arrest is evident in burn-induced anemia.

2.5-fold less LEBs are associated with them. <sentence_start/>Therefore, higher LEB and lower EEB counts associated with sham macrophages indicate a high turnover rate of EEB to LEB differentiation. <sentence_start/>On the contrary, lower LEB and higher EEB counts associated with burn macrophages indicate a dampened turnover rate of LEB to EEB differentiation. <sentence_start/>Whereas, no difference in either Siglec1 expression or EEB association from splenic F4/80 <sup>pos</sup> MØ with two times more LEB association in Burn compared to Sham further strengthens our notion that EBIMØ from spleen and BM are not the same in our burn injury model. <sentence_start/>Therefore, it is plausible that the hampered progress from early to late stage erythroblasts is coupled with Siglec1<sup>lo</sup> EBIMØ impeding BM erythropoiesis. <sentence_start/>This observation is consistent with a previous study done in the model of phenylhydrazine (PHZ)-induced stress erythropoiesis in which the authors found an expansion of F/480 cells expressing Vcam1 and CD169 markers (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1182/blood-2018-06-856831" pmid="30322871" pmcid="PMC6293871" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>From another point of view, one can argue that EEBs express receptors for erythropoietin (Epo-R) and therefore Epo-R mediated signaling mechanisms can be implicated in maturation arrest (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exphem.2017.08.005" pmid="28867537" pmcid="PMC6375690" count="1">37</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, erythropoietin rescues G-CSF induced CFU-E arrest in naïve and splenectomized mice (<citation rid="B38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1749-6632.1994.tb55729.x" pmid="7514380" count="1">38</citation>). <sentence_start/>We acknowledge while this is a possibility, considering burn patients have normal to high erythropoietin levels (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00000658-199303000-00012" pmid="8452408" pmcid="PMC1242783" count="1">1</citation>), Epo-dependent erythropoiesis stages are intact in burn injured subjects (<citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/BCR.0b013e3182642ccd" pmid="23292581" count="1">39</citation>), and that higher doses of Epo promotes migration of BFU-E from BM to spleen preserving robust proliferation (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8462658" count="1">40</citation>), Epo-R defect is highly unlikely as splenic erythropoiesis is augmented in our current study. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, our focus is to decipher myeloid derived EBIMØ phenotypic alterations resulting from burn injury independent of Epo-R signaling.

In hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) mobilization studies, G-CSF can independently increase BM sympathetic tone by increasing nor-epinephrine availability (<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1182/blood-2011-07-367102" pmid="22422821" pmcid="PMC3350363" count="1">41</citation>). <sentence_start/>While Siglec1 is presumed to be involved in EBI forming MØs (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3057" pmid="23502962" pmcid="PMC3983996" count="1">6</citation>), retention of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and erythroid progenitors in the BM is dependent on macrophages expressing Siglec1 (<citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1084/jem.20101688" pmid="21282381" pmcid="PMC3039855" count="1">42</citation>). <sentence_start/>Since sympathetic nervous system (SNS) responses via beta2 and beta3 adrenergic signals are implicated in HSC mobilization (<citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature06685" pmid="18256599" count="1">43</citation>-<citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.10.041" pmid="16439213" count="1">45</citation>), we can speculate that enhanced sympathetic tone following burn (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/SHK.0b013e3181b92340" pmid="20407405" pmcid="PMC2858869" count="1">26</citation>) may explain the reduction in Siglec1 expression in BM EBIMØ. <sentence_start/>We have previously shown that burn injury significantly increased the LSK positive cells in the BM (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1189/jlb.1A0815-377R" pmid="26992433" pmcid="PMC6608024" count="1">4</citation>) and non-specific beta-blockade after burn was effective in partially mitigating this response (<citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/ajpcell.00139.2016" pmid="28031160" pmcid="PMC5401945" count="1">46</citation>). <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, in burn patients, late-stage erythropoiesis remain impaired irrespective of propranolol treatment implying the possibility of beta-2 independent terminal maturation defects (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/BCR.0000000000000592" pmid="28570310" pmcid="PMC5709235" count="1">9</citation>). <sentence_start/>Additionally, our finding of beta3-antagonist -mediated rescue of late erythropoiesis in burn injured mice (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.surg.2017.06.001" pmid="28716301" pmcid="PMC5675564" count="1">20</citation>) supports our hypothetical notion of beta3-adrenergic regulation of Siglec1<sup>+</sup> EBIMØ. <sentence_start/>However, studies using specific pharmacologic antagonists to beta2- and beta3-adrenergic receptors are required to delineate the dual mechanisms down regulating Siglec1 in EBIMØ following burn, which is a major limitation of the current manuscript. <sentence_start/>Further, identification of those intercellular signals that enhance positive interactions between EEBs and Siglec1<sup>++</sup> EBIMØs to augment their maturation to LEBs will remain a key issue for future studies.

Given the intricacies in obtaining the erythroblast island without compromising its integrity, this is our preliminary study observing the down regulation of specific macrophage-associated adhesion molecule that is perturbed by burn injury plausibly impeding erythropoiesis. <sentence_start/>Our results emphasize transient increase in G-CSF cannot drive this persistent anemia in burn patients, Therefore, based on the persistent increase in catecholamines in burn patients and our preliminary data with beta 2 and 3 adrenergic blockade (<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1182/blood-2018-99-112194" count="1">47</citation>) we speculate that sympathetic stimulation of beta3 adrenergic receptors could play a predominant role in burn induced EBIMØ phenotype. <sentence_start/>While current study establishes the premise, targeted knock down of Siglec1 in bone marrow macrophages or studies in beta-3 adrenergic knock out mice are required to further expand our observations, which is beyond the scope of the current manuscript.

Here we have shown that only nucleated erythroblasts (early and late) are tightly associated with EBIMØ (F4/80<sup>+</sup>ERHR3<sup>+</sup>VCAM1<sup>+</sup>Siglec1<sup>+</sup>LY6G<sup>±</sup>), where Siglec1 and Ly6G are predominantly required for EBI integrity in the BM. <sentence_start/>Burn injury significantly diminishes the expression of Siglec1 in BM EBIMØs suggesting a role for the myeloid derived MØ in the maturation of pro erythroblasts into poly/orthochromatic erythroblasts and reticulocytes. <sentence_start/>Having established this methodology to ascertain stage specific dependence of erythroblast maturation on EBIMØ phenotype, detailed functional and mechanistic studies utilizing Siglec1<sup>−/−</sup> and or anti-GCSF and beta3 antagonist treatment in mice subjected to burn injury will be the focus of our future studies.
